newsitem.title: SPAIN: BoS seen waiting on rate cut until later in month.
newsitem.headline: BoS seen waiting on rate cut until later in month.

text.p: Spanish financial markets, rewarded by six official rate cuts in 1996, are betting on yet another reduction this month although no one expects the Bank of Spain to move at its regular tender on Tuesday.

A Reuter poll of 10 experts conducted on Monday ruled out a a cut on Tuesday, but eight economists predicted a cut of 25 to 50 basis points by Christmas, either at the next repo on December 13 or at the final one of the year on December 24.
"The market has already priced in a 50-basis-point cut in December this year and another full point for 1997," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
Better-than-expected October inflation data, when the consumer price index rose a modest 0.1 percent monthly and 3.5 percent yearly, boosted expectations of a fresh rate cut.
But analysts said the Bank of Spain would demand further evidence of moderating inflation before lowering the current 6.75 percent rate.

If the November consumer price index, scheduled for release on December 13, were to decline below the 3.5 percent 1996 target it could justify another reduction, said Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
The Bank of Spain recently revised its forecast on 1996 Spanish inflation downward to 3.4 percent from 3.5.
And Spanish markets, which consider the downtrend in the inflation rate as Spain's ticket to a timely entry into European Monetary Union, have risen fast in anticipation.

At 1230 GMT, long-term bonos future were trading six basis points higher at 112.00. In cash, the 10-year benchmark was flapping around the seven percent yield level, which it had broken on Friday for the first time ever.
Given market contentment, the Bank of Spain has little to lose by postponing the move until the later in the month, analysts said.
"The markets don't think anything will happen tomorrow. The only possible effect would be on the shorter-end," Lumholdt said.

"And if it holds, at the next repo it will have two advantages -- first, more data confirming the downtrend in the inflation and, second, perhaps, the 1997 budget will have been approved," Lumholdt added.
But the market would be disappointed with any further delays.
"If it ends the year having done nothing the market could be disappointed," said Lyonnais' Fernandez.

Still, with the economy expected to pick up in coming months, some economists said the Bank of Spain would likely turn cautious and make sure next year's inflation goal was within reach before moving again.
Jose Luis Alzola, economist at Salomon Brothers in London ruled out any official rate cut this year.
"The Bank of Spain is already targeting next year's inflation goal, which is a steady decline below the three percent level," said Alzola.
"It will cut the key money rate only next year if inflation falls below three percent and wage rises -- a Bank of Spain key concern -- have been tamed," he said.
On October 3, the Bank of Spain last cut its key rate 50 basis points to 6.75 percent. The rate started the year at nine percent.
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
